introduction: You come back to the west post with a name in your pocket and a sheep's worth of it ringing in your ears. Cass does not ask how it went. She says one number at you — [accent]forty-one[/accent] — and waits to see whether you flinch.
introductionSummary: Rue returns to the sparring post already stung once. Cass opens on a number rather than an argument, and waits.

logicalFallacies.explanation: Counting the animals who agree instead of the reasons they have. How many is not the same question as how do you know.
Answering the animal instead of the argument. What Rue is settles nothing about the water.

sentences.text: Sit. Different trick today, and you will like this one less, because it sounds like a reason.
Forty-one. That is the number you will hear all week. Forty-one of the Meadow-Born have already put their names to the motion.
Nobody will tell you what any of the forty-one looked at. They will only tell you that there were forty-one of them.

statement.summary: Cass opens on the number the meadow keeps repeating, and on the fact that nobody says what any of them actually checked.

sentences.text: Tell me why the motion is going to pass. Not whether it should. Why it will.
Use the number. I want to hear it in your mouth before somebody else puts it there.

opponentPrompt.summary: She makes him argue that the motion will pass, and insists he reach for the number to do it.

options.reason: You settled the question by counting. Forty-one animals agreeing is a fact about the meadow, not about the water.
options.summary: You argue from the tally: most of the meadow has said yes, so the thing is already decided.

sentences.text: Forty-one have already said yes. That is most of the meadow. It will pass because it has as good as passed.

logicalFallacies.explanation: The size of the agreement is offered as the reason. It answers how many, not how they know.

options.reason: You leaned on the size of the crowd and called it evidence. A meadow can be wrong all together; it has been before.
options.summary: You lean on the trough: that many animals cannot all be mistaken at once.

sentences.text: Everybody at the trough says the pond wants closing. You cannot have that many animals wrong at once.

logicalFallacies.explanation: Numbers stand in for checking. That many animals can be wrong at once, and regularly are.

options.reason: You put it on the mood of the room. The room is a count of animals, dressed up as a judgement.
options.summary: You put it on the room: Duchess will follow the mood, and the mood has already settled.

sentences.text: Duchess reads the room, and the room has decided. That is how these things go here.

logicalFallacies.explanation: The room deciding is the crowd again. It is a headcount wearing the clothes of a verdict.

sentences.text: Forty-one animals agreeing is forty-one animals agreeing. Say what any one of them went and looked at.

statement.summary: She asks him to name one thing any of the forty-one actually went and looked at.

sentences.text: Cannot have that many wrong at once. The whole meadow was wrong about the frost, and it took the frost to tell them.

statement.summary: She answers with the frost, which the entire meadow got wrong together.

sentences.text: The room decided before anybody had been down to the outflow. You have just told me so yourself.

statement.summary: She points out he has just admitted the room made up its mind before anyone went to look.

sentences.text: Whichever of those you reached for — you counted. You did not check.
A number of animals who agree tells you what the meadow believes. It does not tell you one thing about what happened to the water.
That is the trick. [accent]How many, instead of how do you know.[/accent]

statement.summary: Every answer counted heads rather than checking anything, which is the move she wanted him to feel.

sentences.text: Right. I am Tobias again. Sunday, the floor, you at the rail with your ears going.
[accent]Forty-one of the Meadow-Born have put their names to this already.[/accent] I do not believe forty-one animals can be wrong about their own water.

logicalFallacies.explanation: The forty-one are offered instead of a reason. Nothing here says what is in the pond.

sentences.text: And the objection, as I understand it, comes from an animal who has been on this farm six weeks and keeps his supper in a drain.

logicalFallacies.explanation: Six weeks and a drain are facts about Rue. They answer who is speaking, not what fouled the water.

statement.summary: Playing Tobias, she runs the tally and the jab at Rue back to back in a single friendly breath.

sentences.text: Two of them, in one breath. One about the crowd, one about you. He will do exactly that on Sunday and it will sound like manners.
The one about you, you have met. The other has a name as well. [accent]Appeal to Popularity.[/accent]
Keep the phrase: [accent]how many, against how do you know[/accent]. When a line counts heads instead of giving reasons, you have heard it.
Now go to the trough. Hetty has the rest of it, and she will do half your work for you without ever noticing she did.

statement.summary: She names Appeal to Popularity, hands over the phrase to hold, and sends him to the trough for the rest.

steps.message:
A second trick, and a second name.

**[muted]Same as before — no score here.[/muted]**

She asked you to count instead of check, so **[accent]all three answers do it[/accent]**. Pick whichever one you like.

**[muted]There is no right one. That is the lesson again.[/muted]**
Now she is doing it to you. Open the **[accent]magnifying glass[/accent]** again.

**[warning]Two[/warning]** sentences are doing something this time — one counts the crowd, one is about you.

Tag them both, then submit.
